title: CGM Interpretation: Find the Pattern Before Changing the Dose
bottomLine: CGM is most useful when the NP interprets time in range, time below range, time above range, variability, overnight/post-meal patterns and data quality together. Do not adjust insulin from one arrow or one day without identifying a repeatable pattern and the behavioural/meal/activity context.
recognize: Time below range and severe/nocturnal lows usually deserve attention before chasing modest hyperglycemia.
Sensor compression, lag during rapid glucose change and incomplete wear can create misleading patterns.
differentiate: GMI is an estimate from sensor data and can differ from laboratory A1C.
A postprandial spike, dawn phenomenon, missed bolus, basal insufficiency and rebound after hypoglycemia require different changes even if average glucose is similar.
assessment: Review sensor wear completeness, insulin regimen/pump/AID settings, meals, activity, alcohol, illness, menstruation/pregnancy, hypoglycemia awareness and whether symptoms match sensor readings.
workup: Use a sufficiently representative CGM interval when possible and inspect ambulatory glucose profile/patterns rather than isolated screenshots.
Confirm glucose with capillary testing when device guidance requires it or symptoms and sensor readings do not agree.
management: Prioritize hypoglycemia prevention, then make one or a small number of pattern-based insulin/behaviour adjustments at a time.
AID users require review of settings, infusion delivery and user behaviour before manual overcorrection.
medicationSafety: Avoid insulin stacking based on trend arrows alone.
Repeated nocturnal or severe hypoglycemia requires de-intensification/regimen redesign and rescue-glucagon planning rather than simply telling the patient to eat more.
redFlags: Pregnancy with recurrent out-of-range glucose requiring specialist adjustment
counselling: Teach trend-arrow limits, alarm fatigue prevention and which patterns justify contacting the diabetes team.
followUp: Reassess the same CGM metrics after changes and confirm improvement without increasing hypoglycemia burden.
examTrap: Increasing basal insulin because morning glucose is high without checking whether overnight hypoglycemia, missed evening bolus or dawn phenomenon explains the pattern.
oneLinePearl: CGM treatment changes should follow repeated patterns, not single dots.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Blood Glucose Monitoring Update

title: Insulin Initiation and Titration: Match the Insulin to the Glucose Pattern
bottomLine: Start insulin when the clinical indication requires it, then titrate the insulin component that matches the abnormal glucose pattern. Basal insulin targets fasting physiology; prandial insulin targets meal excursions; correction insulin treats current hyperglycemia and must not become a substitute for an inadequate scheduled regimen.
recognize: Severe symptomatic hyperglycemia, catabolic symptoms or metabolic decompensation may require insulin promptly regardless of the A1C number.
Basal overinsulinization is suggested when fasting glucose is acceptable but overnight or fasting hypoglycemia occurs while daytime/post-meal hyperglycemia persists.
differentiate: Type 1 diabetes always requires basal insulin coverage; type 2 insulin initiation is individualized.
Fasting hyperglycemia calls for basal review, whereas isolated postprandial elevations usually require meal/bolus strategy rather than simply increasing basal insulin.
assessment: Review diabetes type, current glucose pattern, A1C reliability, hypoglycemia risk, meals, renal function, frailty, weight goals, cost/coverage, injection skills and pregnancy.
workup: Use fasting and/or CGM/SMBG patterns to guide titration; evaluate ketosis/electrolytes urgently when metabolic decompensation is possible.
management: Use a validated basal-insulin initiation/titration approach and individualize targets; add prandial insulin or other therapy when fasting glucose is controlled but A1C/post-meal patterns remain above goal.
Teach self-titration only when the patient can use the algorithm safely and has clear hypoglycemia instructions.
medicationSafety: Insulin dose changes must account for renal decline, reduced intake, acute illness, steroids and activity changes.
Do not stop all insulin in type 1 diabetes because the patient is NPO; use a clinician-directed basal strategy.
redFlags: Rapid renal decline with insulin accumulation
counselling: Teach injection/device technique, site rotation, storage, hypoglycemia treatment, driving safety and sick-day rules.
followUp: Review glucose patterns soon after initiation/titration until a stable regimen is reached.
examTrap: Increasing basal insulin repeatedly to fix post-meal hyperglycemia while fasting glucose is already at target and overnight lows are appearing.
oneLinePearl: Titrate the insulin that matches the timing of the glucose problem.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Appendix 9 Insulin Initiation and Titration

title: Thyroid Cancer Follow-Up: Risk-Adapt Surveillance Over Time
bottomLine: Differentiated thyroid-cancer surveillance is risk-adapted and dynamic. Follow the specialist treatment history, thyroglobulin/antibody context, neck imaging and individualized TSH target; do not order the same scan/lab schedule forever after every thyroid cancer.
recognize: Recurrence risk changes with pathology, stage, treatment, postoperative response and subsequent biochemical/imaging findings.
Thyroglobulin interpretation depends on remaining thyroid tissue, antibodies, assay context and treatment history.
differentiate: A detectable thyroglobulin does not have the same meaning after lobectomy as after total thyroidectomy/ablation.
TSH suppression intensity must balance recurrence risk with AF/bone and other harms.
assessment: Review surgery/pathology, radioiodine, current levothyroxine/TSH target, prior thyroglobulin/antibodies, neck ultrasound, symptoms, pregnancy plans and treatment complications.
workup: Use risk-adapted thyroglobulin/antibody and neck-ultrasound surveillance; additional CT/MRI/RAI/PET is driven by biochemical or structural concern rather than routine use in every survivor.
management: Maintain levothyroxine/TSH goals appropriate to current recurrence risk and response category.
New biochemical/structural concern requires endocrinology/thyroid-oncology reassessment rather than empiric dose escalation alone.
medicationSafety: Excessive chronic TSH suppression can worsen atrial arrhythmia and bone loss; under-replacement can undermine the intended oncologic plan.
Pregnancy requires coordinated thyroid hormone monitoring/adjustment.
redFlags: New neck mass or progressive nodes
Rising thyroglobulin trend with appropriate assay context
counselling: Explain why surveillance intensity may decrease after an excellent response and why TSH targets can change over time.
followUp: Assign ownership between endocrine/oncology/primary care and document the current response/risk category and next tests.
examTrap: Keeping every low-risk thyroid-cancer survivor maximally TSH-suppressed indefinitely without reassessing recurrence response and treatment harms.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid-cancer follow-up evolves with response; surveillance is not one permanent template.
sourceBasis: Cancer Care Ontario Thyroid Cancer Pathway

title: Hypoparathyroidism: Prevent Symptoms Without Causing Hypercalciuria
bottomLine: Chronic hypoparathyroidism is not treated by pushing serum calcium to the high-normal range. Use calcium/active vitamin D and adjunctive strategies to control symptoms while avoiding hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis and renal decline; acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is an emergency pathway.
recognize: Perioral/finger paresthesias, cramps, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation can occur with clinically important hypocalcemia.
Low/inappropriately normal PTH with hypocalcemia after neck surgery is a common pattern.
differentiate: Vitamin D deficiency, CKD, severe hypomagnesemia and other causes can produce hypocalcemia without primary hypoparathyroidism.
Serum calcium control can look acceptable while urinary calcium remains excessive.
assessment: Assess symptoms, neck surgery/radiation, medications, calcium/vitamin D intake, renal stones, renal function, magnesium and pregnancy.
workup: Use corrected or ionized calcium as appropriate, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR and PTH; monitor urine calcium/renal imaging when clinically indicated for chronic therapy.
management: Use divided calcium and active vitamin D therapy individualized to symptoms and biochemical goals; correct magnesium deficiency and consider thiazide/dietary strategies for hypercalciuria where appropriate.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium and treatment of the cause.
medicationSafety: Overtreatment can cause hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria and kidney injury.
Thiazides, PPIs and other medications can alter calcium/magnesium handling and require review.
counselling: Teach symptom recognition and that the goal is safe symptom control, not the highest possible calcium value.
followUp: Monitor serum/urine/renal parameters at intervals matched to treatment stability and after dose changes.
examTrap: Escalating calcium until serum values are high-normal while ignoring hypercalciuria and kidney risk.
oneLinePearl: In hypoparathyroidism, calcium must be high enough for safety but not so high that the kidneys pay the price.

title: Vitamin D: Test and Treat When There Is a Clinical Reason
bottomLine: Do not screen every healthy adult for vitamin D deficiency or use megadose vitamin D as a general disease-prevention strategy. Test when deficiency risk or a bone/endocrine indication makes the result actionable, then replace according to severity/context and reassess only when it will change management.
recognize: Risk is higher with malabsorption/bariatric surgery, severe dietary limitation, selected bone/endocrine disease, institutionalization/low sun exposure and medications that alter vitamin D metabolism.
Severe deficiency can contribute to osteomalacia, muscle weakness and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
differentiate: Low bone density is not automatically caused by vitamin D deficiency.
Routine supplementation recommendations for older adults/bone health are different from treatment of documented severe deficiency.
assessment: Assess diet/supplements, fracture/osteoporosis risk, malabsorption/bariatric history, kidney/liver disease, calcium disorders, medications and symptoms suggesting osteomalacia.
workup: Order 25-hydroxyvitamin D when a defined indication exists; pair with calcium/phosphate/PTH/renal or other testing when the clinical syndrome warrants it.
Avoid repeated levels in stable low-risk people when the result will not alter care.
management: Use Health Canada/Osteoporosis Canada nutrition guidance for routine bone health and individualized replacement for true deficiency/risk states.
Investigate malabsorption or secondary causes when levels fail to respond as expected.
medicationSafety: Avoid intermittent very-high-dose regimens without a specific indication because excessive vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia and may increase falls in some settings.
Account for calcium intake and renal/granulomatous disease when supplementing.
counselling: Explain that more vitamin D is not automatically better and supplementation should match the clinical indication.
followUp: Repeat levels selectively after treatment of significant deficiency or when absorption/adherence remains uncertain.
examTrap: Ordering annual vitamin D levels and high-dose supplements for every healthy adult without a risk factor or management-changing question.
oneLinePearl: Vitamin D testing is useful when the result changes care—not as a routine wellness panel.
sourceBasis: Osteoporosis Canada 2026 calcium/vitamin D position update

title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Find the Mechanism Behind the Fragile Bone
bottomLine: Low BMD or fragility fracture can reflect primary osteoporosis or a secondary metabolic bone disorder. Assess fracture pattern, medications and secondary causes, then use calcium/phosphate/renal/alkaline phosphatase/TSH and selected vitamin D/PTH or other tests to identify a treatable mechanism before simply adding bone medication.
recognize: Glucocorticoids, hyperparathyroidism, malabsorption, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, CKD and some hematologic disorders can cause secondary bone loss.
Osteomalacia may produce bone pain/weakness and biochemical mineralization abnormalities rather than only low BMD.
differentiate: Osteoporosis is a fracture-risk disorder; osteomalacia is defective mineralization; CKD-mineral/bone disorder has a different biochemical/pathophysiologic framework.
A normal BMD does not exclude fragility risk after a characteristic low-trauma fracture.
assessment: Review fracture history, height loss, falls, steroid/antiepileptic/aromatase therapies, nutrition, GI/bariatric history, kidney/endocrine disease, menstrual/androgen status and family history.
workup: Use BMD/fracture-risk assessment and targeted secondary-cause labs according to Osteoporosis Canada guidance; spine imaging is selected when occult vertebral fracture is plausible.
Abnormal calcium/phosphate/PTH/renal patterns require mechanism-specific evaluation rather than routine osteoporosis treatment alone.
management: Correct secondary causes, optimize nutrition/exercise/falls prevention and use pharmacotherapy according to fracture risk and underlying bone disorder.
Refer unusual, severe, premenopausal/young, CKD-related or treatment-refractory disease to appropriate specialty care.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonate/denosumab/anabolic therapy selection depends on renal function, calcium/vitamin D status, fracture risk, duration strategy and contraindications.
Stopping denosumab without an antiresorptive transition can produce rebound vertebral-fracture risk.
counselling: Explain that bone fragility may have a correctable cause and that treatment is broader than calcium tablets.
followUp: Track fracture risk, adherence/tolerance and secondary-cause correction; repeat BMD only at intervals that can change management.
examTrap: Starting osteoporosis medication after a fragility fracture without reviewing chronic glucocorticoids, hyperparathyroidism or other secondary causes.
oneLinePearl: Before treating weak bone, ask why the bone became weak.

title: Pituitary Adenoma: Hormone Excess, Hormone Loss, or Mass Effect?
bottomLine: A pituitary adenoma matters because it may secrete hormone, compress visual/neurologic structures or impair normal pituitary function. Define those three domains before management; sudden severe headache/visual/ophthalmoplegic symptoms with adrenal compromise can represent pituitary apoplexy and require emergency care.
recognize: Prolactin excess, acromegaly, Cushing disease, hyperthyroidism from TSH secretion or hypopituitarism produce different syndromes.
Bitemporal visual field loss, headache or cranial-nerve dysfunction suggests mass effect.
differentiate: Medication/stalk-effect hyperprolactinemia can mimic prolactinoma; hook effect and macroprolactin can complicate interpretation.
Central hypothyroidism/adrenal insufficiency may have inappropriately normal TSH/cortisol patterns and cannot be screened with TSH alone.
assessment: Assess vision/fields, headache, menstrual/sexual function, galactorrhea, growth/acromegalic features, cortisol symptoms, thyroid symptoms and signs of pituitary hormone deficiency.
workup: Use pituitary MRI and targeted hormone testing; evaluate adrenal function before starting thyroid replacement when central hypopituitarism is possible.
Formal visual-field testing is indicated when the lesion threatens the optic apparatus.
management: Prolactinomas often respond to dopamine-agonist therapy; other functional/mass lesions frequently require endocrinology/neurosurgery management.
Treat pituitary hormone deficiencies and urgent apoplexy through specialist/acute-care pathways.
medicationSafety: Starting levothyroxine before recognizing untreated central adrenal insufficiency can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Dopamine-agonist treatment requires monitoring of symptom/hormone/tumour response and tolerability.
counselling: Explain which symptoms suggest hormone excess/loss versus mass effect and why multiple hormones may need reassessment.
followUp: Track tumour size, visual function and hormone response through endocrinology; surveillance interval depends on lesion type/treatment.
examTrap: Starting thyroid hormone in a patient with suspected panhypopituitarism before assessing adrenal reserve.
oneLinePearl: Pituitary lesions are evaluated on three axes: secretion, deficiency, and compression.

title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy: Choose for Complications, Goals, and Long-Term Use
bottomLine: Obesity pharmacotherapy is chronic disease treatment, not a short-term willpower aid. Select therapy using adiposity-related complications, goals, contraindications, pregnancy plans, access/cost and patient preference; continue effective therapy long term when benefit outweighs harm and avoid stigmatizing BMI-only decisions.
recognize: Type 2 diabetes, OSA, hypertension, MASLD, osteoarthritis and other adiposity-related complications can strengthen the indication for treatment.
Stopping effective anti-obesity therapy commonly leads to weight regain because obesity is chronic and biologically defended.
differentiate: Medication selection differs from treating an eating disorder or unexplained pathologic weight change.
BMI alone is an imperfect measure; central adiposity and obesity-related complications matter in the Canadian framework.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight; assess complications, eating-disorder symptoms, pregnancy plans, current medications, BP/HR, gallbladder/pancreatitis history as relevant, mental health, access and treatment goals.
workup: Screen for obesity-related complications and plausible secondary contributors based on history rather than ordering broad endocrine testing routinely.
management: Use lifestyle/behavioural support plus evidence-based pharmacotherapy selected according to current Obesity Canada guidance; consider metabolic/bariatric referral when indicated and desired.
Evaluate response by health/function/complication outcomes as well as weight change.
medicationSafety: Review product-specific contraindications/interactions and pregnancy/lactation; anti-obesity drugs are not used during pregnancy for weight loss.
Escalate severe persistent GI symptoms, dehydration or possible gallbladder/pancreatic complications according to the agent and clinical picture.
counselling: Use person-first non-stigmatizing language and set realistic long-term goals rather than framing success as reaching a 'normal BMI'.
followUp: Reassess benefit, adverse effects, comorbidity outcomes, adherence and affordability; change therapy when response or tolerability is inadequate.
examTrap: Requiring a patient to fail repeated diet-only attempts before offering evidence-based obesity pharmacotherapy despite clinically important complications.
oneLinePearl: Obesity medication is chronic disease therapy; select it for the patient's health goals and complications.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada Adult Clinical Practice Guideline — Pharmacotherapy updated 2025
